definition: Albert One is an artificial intelligence chatbot created by Robby Garner and designed to mimic the way humans make conversations using a multi-faceted approach in natural language programming.
details: Albert One is an artificial intelligence chatbot created by Robby Garner and designed to mimic the way humans make conversations using a multi-faceted approach in natural language programming.

explainer.lead: Albert One was a chatbot built by Robby Garner to imitate human conversation through several cooperating techniques rather than one single method. It combined ELIZA-like programs with a growing collection of human statements and replies, and won the Loebner Prize Contest in both 1998 and 1999.

tiers.eli5: Albert One was a computer program that chatted with people, a bit like a group of friends working together to come up with one answer. Different helpers handled different parts of the conversation, while a big collection of things people say and possible replies provided more ideas. Its approach was successful enough to win a contest for talking computer programs two years in a row.
tiers.practitioner: Treat Albert One as a hierarchical, multi-subsystem chatterbot rather than a single learned language model. Its pattern coordinates ELIZA-like modules and helper applications with a statement–reply library, using additional database queries and assertions to determine each response. Parts were deployed online from 1995 to gather examples of what people would say, so the conversation data and the subsystem coordination are both central to understanding its behavior.
tiers.paperLevel: Albert One can be described as a hierarchical composite chatterbot: given a user utterance u, multiple subsystems, a stimulus–response library, and additional database queries and assertions jointly determine a response r. Its named components include a version of ELIZA, another ELIZA-like bot called Elivs, and several helper applications. The available description does not specify a scoring function or formal response-selection algorithm.

usedIn.name: Loebner Prize Contest
usedIn.detail: Its statement-and-reply approach was tested in the 1994–1997 contests, and Albert One won in 1998 and 1999.

usedIn.name: Internet chatterbot interactions
usedIn.detail: Parts of Albert were deployed online beginning in 1995 to gather information about what people would say to a chatterbot.

components.name: Hierarchical helper applications
components.detail: Several applications worked together in a hierarchical arrangement to coordinate Albert One's behavior.

components.name: ELIZA subsystem
components.detail: A version of ELIZA, the therapist program, formed one of the conversational subsystems.

components.name: Elivs
components.detail: This second ELIZA-like bot contributed another conversational component.

components.name: Stimulus–response library
components.detail: A large database associated human statements with possible replies.

components.name: Database queries and assertions
components.detail: Additional queries and assertions were tested to help determine each response.

flow: A person enters a statement for Albert One to answer.
The hierarchically arranged subsystems and helper applications process the conversational input.
ELIZA-like components and the statement–reply library contribute to response generation.
Further database queries and assertions are tested to arrive at a response.
Albert One returns the resulting reply to the person.
explainer.origin: Robby Garner created Albert One, with parts deployed on the internet beginning in 1995 to collect examples of human statements to a chatterbot. Its statement-and-reply database component was tested at the 1994–1997 Loebner Prize contests.
explainer.lineage: Albert was the first of Garner's multifaceted bots. He later developed networked examples of this kind of hierarchical “glue” at The Turing Hub.
explainer.whyItMatters: Albert One illustrates an early composite approach to conversation in which multiple bots, helper programs, and response data cooperate. Its consecutive Loebner Prize wins in 1998 and 1999 made that approach especially notable among chatterbots of its time.
